evidence.text: Architecture and environmental proxies support different questions. A coincident drought is not a sufficient political explanation.

production.text: A large capital required provisioning; severe drought is a proposed stress on those systems, not a complete explanation of political action.

coordination.text: Palace, temples, archives and provisioning connected recurring work. Proxy evidence for moisture stress is separate from proof of how institutions responded.

question: Does evidence for drought explain a political ending?
summary: Hattusha was a place of government, worship, building and provisioning before it became a problem of collapse. Its royal administration depended on people moving food and maintaining institutions across a changing city. Evidence for severe drought near the political transformation adds a possible stress to that history. It does not turn the end of the central administration into the disappearance of everyone in the region.

sections.title: A capital coordinated more than royal display
sections.text: The DAI describes a capital and cult centre with a palace, temples and cuneiform archives. These institutions coordinated decisions, ritual obligations and resources. Maintaining their buildings required recurring work and supplies, connecting royal authority with builders and providers. The broad c. 1650–1180 BCE capital orientation is separate from this dossier’s 13th-century case. It does not describe the settlement’s whole lifespan or an unchanging arrangement of districts.

citations.locator: Project overview: capital, cult, palace and archives

sections.title: Houses and open ground belong in the city
sections.text: Excavation in the northern Lower City traces residential construction from the earlier kārum period into Hittite phases and identifies housing alongside an official building. Schachner’s later synthesis describes settled areas moving and changing intensity through time. Dense districts could stand beside older ruins or open ground. A combined site plan is therefore a record assembled from different phases. It should not be read as a complete map of all the people, streets and buildings operating on the day the central government withdrew.

sections.title: Food could be stored, but resilience had limits
sections.text: The drought study discusses cereals as a food and tax base, with storage helping communities manage variable harvests. Repeated shortages pose a different problem from one bad season: using stored food leaves less protection if another crop fails. This is a proposed mechanism linking environmental stress to provisioning and political vulnerability. It is not a calculation of the grain left in every household or proof that all districts lacked alternatives. Distribution, access and decisions still matter when interpreting a material shortfall.

sections.title: The tree record has its own location and clock
sections.text: Manning and colleagues analyzed juniper timbers recovered at Gordion, about 230 km west of Hattusha. Ring widths and carbon isotopes indicate moisture conditions, rather than directly measuring decisions at the capital. They identify a severe dry episode around 1198–1196 BCE, with a ±3-year dating uncertainty. The central estimate falls just after the case endpoint of about 1200 BCE. The dating uncertainty can overlap that endpoint, so the wider reference frame shows the episode with its own dates. The authors acknowledge that direct causation remains unproved; abandonment of the royal centre also needs to be distinguished from later burning.

returnPrompt: Which dated evidence would help connect a regional food stress with the withdrawal of a particular institution?

deeperReading.title: Separate a withdrawal from an empty landscape
deeperReading.text: A central administration can cease to operate while people and practices continue at other scales. The drought paper distinguishes the emptied royal centre and later burning, and discusses continuation and adaptation elsewhere in former Hittite territories. Schachner’s archaeological abstract offers another reason to resist a single dramatic snapshot: Hattusha’s occupied areas had changed long before the final political transition. A next investigation should ask which buildings stopped functioning, which activities moved and which evidence dates each change. The end of a document series is a consequential institutional event, but not a census proving that every resident left at once.

deeperReading.title: A proxy is evidence with an argument behind it
deeperReading.text: Tree growth responds to more than one influence. The researchers compare samples, remove growth trends and use isotope evidence to strengthen the moisture interpretation. Their record is not a rainfall gauge at Hattusha, and its precision is not unlimited. A plausible causal account must connect this regional stress with dated provisioning, institutions and human decisions. The diagram keeps those steps separate instead of drawing an automatic arrow from drought to collapse. Household access to stores, labor demands and different coping strategies remain questions for further evidence rather than reconstructed conversations among imaginary residents.

evidenceReading.title: From a measured proxy to a historical claim
evidenceReading.introduction: These are source paraphrases. None is a quotation from a Hittite witness describing the last day of the capital.

items.label: Where the timbers were recovered
items.text: The analyzed juniper timbers came from archaeological contexts at Gordion, west of Hattusha; growth rings preserve an earlier environmental record.
items.interpretation: The place and date of timber recovery, the years in which the trees grew and the city whose history is being discussed are different units. Gordion is not silently relabelled Hattusha.

items.label: What the date can support
items.text: The paper identifies unusually severe dryness around 1198–1196 BCE, with ±3-year dating uncertainty, and explicitly says it cannot establish direct causation.
items.interpretation: The dates sharpen a proposed historical connection without proving one event caused every political change. The figure here contains no invented annual rainfall values.

items.label: What a whole-site plan conceals
items.text: The archaeological synthesis describes continuous changes in occupied areas and calls the overall plan a modern reconstruction.
items.interpretation: Treat a plan as evidence to date and interpret. Do not turn every visible foundation into simultaneous late-13th-century occupation.
